phase3_findings.description: The denylist refusal text from _refuse_denied_function ends 'refused by the read-only guard', but with rules configured and database.read_only = false it is reached through RlsGuardRunner._refuse_denied_functions while ReadOnlyGuardRunner is not in the chain, so the message names the wrong guard.

Docstrings describe the routine check as matching 'a routine defined in the database', wider than the lookup (PostgreSQL skips pg_catalog/information_schema; MySQL checks only ROUTINE_TYPE = 'FUNCTION'). Instances: relations.py 118-120, __init__.py 17-18 and 136-138.

Module docstring lines 11-13 say 'the guard also applies the read-only guard's function denylist' right after naming the read-only guard, so 'the guard' reads as the read-only guard instead of RlsGuardRunner.

The changelog fragment's opening sentence says RLS 'no longer lets PostgreSQL child tables or database functions read past your rules'; the routine check only sees names written before '(', so functions reached by attribute notation or operators/casts still run, as the PR's own docs record.

The diff edits the existing SQLite test test_sqlite_missing_table_list_capability_blocks_execution (adds a comment, tightens the match), departing from criterion 7's wording that existing SQLite RLS tests pass unmodified; the old assertion still passes at head.

The require_base_tables contract now also requires child-table and routine refusal and fail-closed lookups, but _declares_relation_check only confirms the parameter exists, so a custom runner written to the earlier contract passes startup and skips the new checks.

_refuse_database_routines treats every non-postgres dialect as MySQL; only the caller's gate at relations.py line 124 keeps other dialects out, while the sibling _verify_relations raises RlsError for an unknown dialect.

No test exercises the case-insensitive predicates in the routine lookup SQL (lower(p.proname::text) = ANY(%s), LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (...)); the fake cursor lowercases names itself and connector tests use lowercase names.

report:
## Verdict: APPROVE with notes (no finding at the critical threshold; one Important and seven Suggestion findings, five checklist items inconclusive)
The PR is ready to merge: all 12 acceptance criteria and every other checklist item that could be settled passed, and no reviewer found a Critical defect, though the changelog headline overstates the function check and should be narrowed before release.
Rule applied: rule 6 — findings below the threshold and INCONCLUSIVE checklist items remain → APPROVE with notes

## Code Review Findings

### 🟠 Important / Major

1. `changelog.d/325.security.md` lines 1–2 open with "Row-level security no longer lets PostgreSQL child tables or database functions read past your rules". The function half of that sentence is wider than the code. `_called_names` in `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` only collects names written directly before `(`, so a PostgreSQL function can still run without call syntax, for example through attribute notation or a user-defined operator or cast. The PR's own external and internal docs list attribute notation as still open, and lines 11–12 of the fragment qualify it ("SQL Lens checks only names written as calls"), but the release-note headline does not. Narrow the first sentence to calls written with call syntax. (raised by 1/6 agents) <!-- inertness: first-conjunct=held limb-one=held limb-two=not-held; evidence: the finding disputes only the sentence, not the guard's coverage, and rewording it changes no output; git grep of scripts/ and .github/ for changelog.d finds only scripts/changelog.py, which copies fragment text into CHANGELOG.md and decides no program behavior; a release note is read outside the repository -->

### 🟡 Suggestion / Minor (7)

<details><summary>7 items</summary>

1. `src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py` lines 559–562: the denylist refusal text from `_refuse_denied_function` ends "refused by the read-only guard". With rules configured and `database.read_only = false`, `RlsGuardRunner._refuse_denied_functions` (`src/sqllens/safety/__init__.py` lines 203–208) now reaches this message although `ReadOnlyGuardRunner` is not in the chain, so the message names the wrong guard. The refusal is still a structured `UnsafeSqlError` that names the function. (raised by 1/6 agents)
2. Docstrings describe the routine check as matching "a routine defined in the database", which is wider than the lookup. The lookup skips `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` on PostgreSQL and checks only `ROUTINE_TYPE = 'FUNCTION'` on MySQL. Instances: `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` lines 118–120 (`verify_base_tables`), `src/sqllens/safety/__init__.py` lines 17–18 (module docstring) and lines 136–138 (`RlsGuardRunner`). The `_refuse_database_routines` docstring and both docs state the scope correctly. (raised by 1/6 agents) <!-- inertness: first-conjunct=held limb-one=held limb-two=held; evidence: docstring wording only, no output or branch depends on it; no tool or agent-loaded file reads these docstrings; internal docstrings are not printed or published -->
3. `src/sqllens/safety/__init__.py` lines 11–13: "With rules configured, the guard also applies the read-only guard's function denylist" follows a sentence about the read-only guard, so "the guard" reads as the read-only guard. Name `RlsGuardRunner`, which runs this check even when `read_only` is false. (raised by 1/6 agents) <!-- inertness: first-conjunct=held limb-one=held limb-two=held; evidence: module docstring wording only; no tool or agent-loaded file reads it; it is not printed or published -->
4. `tests/unit/test_rls_views.py` lines 394–395: the diff edits the existing SQLite test `test_sqlite_missing_table_list_capability_blocks_execution`, adding a comment and tightening its `match` to "could not verify relation types; query blocked". Criterion 7 says SQLite's existing RLS tests pass unmodified. The old assertion still passes at head, so the edit only adds strictness, but it departs from the criterion's wording. (raised by 1/6 agents)
5. `src/sqllens/agent/capabilities/sql_runner/base.py` lines 22–34: the `require_base_tables` docstring now also requires child-table refusal, routine-name refusal and fail-closed catalog lookups. The only structural check, `_declares_relation_check` in `src/sqllens/safety/__init__.py`, confirms only that `run_sql` declares the parameter. A custom runner written to the earlier contract would pass startup and skip the new checks. The shipped SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL runners all route through `verify_base_tables`. (raised by 1/6 agents)
6. `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` lines 237–262: `_refuse_database_routines` treats every dialect that is not `"postgres"` as MySQL and sends it the `information_schema.ROUTINES` query. Only the caller's gate at line 124 keeps other dialects out, while the sibling `_verify_relations` raises `RlsError` for an unknown dialect. (raised by 1/6 agents)
7. `tests/unit/test_rls_views.py` lines 458–491: no test exercises the case-insensitive predicates in the routine lookup SQL (`lower(p.proname::text) = ANY(%s)` and `LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (...)` in `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` lines 251 and 260). The fake cursor lowercases names itself, and the connector tests use all-lowercase names, so removing either `lower()` would leave every test passing. (raised by 1/6 agents)

</details>

### ℹ️ Informational — Deferred (5)

<details><summary>5 items</summary>

- VC-11: INCONCLUSIVE (important) — The internal doc says MySQL partitions are selected inside their table (`FROM orders PARTITION (p0)`) so the rewrite still sees and filters the table, i.e. sqlglot's MySQL parse of a `PARTITION (...)` clause keeps the table node that `apply_rls` scopes and does not error or hide it. [docs/internal/database-connectors/row-level-security.md:43]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  Traced by reading only; I could not execute sqlglot (no run tool), and the rejection line does not cover this claim. In the installed sqlglot parser (.venv/.../sqlglot/parser.py:1953, 5251-5253) SUPPORTS_PARTITION_SELECTION defaults False, and neither dialects/mysql.py nor any dialect overrides it. So for `FROM orders PARTITION (p0)` the PARTITION clause is not parsed as a partition. PARTITION is in ID_VAR_TOKENS (parser.py:823), so _parse_table_alias (parser.py:4415-4445) most likely reads it as the table alias with column list (p0). If so, the exp.Table node for orders is kept and no ParseError is raised, so apply_rls (rls.py:282-297) would inject the predicate. The qualifier would be table.alias_or_name, i.e. `PARTITION`. The regenerated SQL would then probably be `orders AS PARTITION(p0) WHERE PARTITION.<col> = ...`. That is likely invalid MySQL (it fails, not leaks), and it is not the partition selection the doc describes. No test in the repo exercises this input (grep of tests found none for MySQL PARTITION). The claim that the table is seen and not hidden is plausible, but the doc's wording of how it works is unverified. Without running `sqlglot.parse_one('SELECT * FROM orders PARTITION (p0)', dialect='mysql')` and `apply_rls` I cannot settle it. Command not run: that parse plus apply_rls with a rule on orders under dialect mysql.

  </details>

- VC-13: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — The internal doc says sqlglot renames `strpos` to `StrPosition` and parses `replace` as a keyword, justifying token-based collection. [docs/internal/database-connectors/row-level-security.md:45]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  No installed sqlglot source was found (globs for sqlglot/expressions.py under the repo and .venv returned nothing; a wider search timed out), so I could not read exp.StrPosition's parse names. The REPLACE half is pinned: tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:597-604 asserts the postgres tokenizer's token for REPLACE is neither VAR nor IDENTIFIER. The strpos half is only indirectly supported: test_rls_views.py:619-629 shows a rewritten strpos call executes under a different name and the lookup excludes 'str_position', but that does not show that strpos parses to StrPosition. Missing evidence: sqlglot's expressions.py for the supported range (>=25.0,<31).

  </details>

- VC-31: INCONCLUSIVE (important) — _called_names relies on sqlglot.Dialect.get_or_raise(dialect) returning a Dialect instance whose class exposes tokenizer_class.KEYWORDS (a mapping keyed by upper-case keyword text) and whose instance has a tokenize(sql) method returning Token objects with token_type and text, across the supported sqlglot>=25.0,<31 range. [src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:94]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  relations.py:94-96 uses Dialect.get_or_raise(dialect), type(d).tokenizer_class.KEYWORDS and d.tokenize(sql). pyproject.toml:44 allows sqlglot>=25.0,<31. Verified only against installed sqlglot 30.26.0 (.venv): dialect.py:1047 get_or_raise classmethod returning Dialect, dialect.py:903 tokenizer_class = Tokenizer, tokens.py:229 KEYWORDS dict, dialect.py:1286 tokenize(sql)->list[Token], tokenizer_core.py:478-522 Token with token_type and text. No sqlglot 25.x-29.x source was available to read, so the lower and middle parts of the range are unverified. I did not check that KEYWORDS keys are upper-case.

  </details>

- VC-32: INCONCLUSIVE (important) — Every token sqlglot emits for a name written immediately before '(' (an unquoted function name, a double-quoted or backtick-quoted identifier, or a keyword-tokenized built-in such as REPLACE) is either typed VAR/IDENTIFIER or has text whose upper-case form is a key in the dialect tokenizer's KEYWORDS, and for a quoted identifier token.text is the name without its quote characters; a call name that falls outside both is not collected and so not looked up. [src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:98]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  Read src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:84-107: _called_names keeps a token before L_PAREN when its type is VAR/IDENTIFIER or token.text.upper() is in the tokenizer KEYWORDS. The claim concerns how sqlglot's tokenizer assigns token_type and text. In the installed sqlglot (.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sqlglot/tokens.py) the scanning methods (_scan_keywords, _scan_var, _scan_identifier, _add) are not present in Python source; the scan loop is a compiled tokenizer (rust or compiled). No tokenizer source was readable in any available sqlglot install, and I had no way to run the tokenizer to inspect token_type/text for the hinted inputs. This is an absolute claim (every token), so it cannot be settled from the caller's code alone. Not run: sqlglot.Dialect.get_or_raise('postgres'/'mysql').tokenize on the hinted inputs.

  </details>

- VC-52: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — The test comment states apply_rls's postgres output for strpos(...) emits STRPOS on sqlglot 25.x and POSITION on 30.x, and the test asserts the looked-up names include 'position' or 'strpos' and not 'str_position'. [tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:625]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  Test at tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:619-629 asserts ({'position','strpos'} & set(params[0])) and 'str_position' not in params[0], matching the claim. 30.x half confirmed: installed sqlglot 30.21.0 (implement-304 sg3021) generators/postgres.py:394 has exp.StrPosition: strposition_sql(self, e, func_name='POSITION'). pyproject pins sqlglot>=25.0,<31. The 25.x half (emits STRPOS) could not be verified: no sqlglot 25.x source exists in any local venv or the supplied artifacts (only 30.x installs found). Missing evidence: sqlglot 25.x postgres generator source.

  </details>

</details>

acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured on PostgreSQL, a statement that references a relation recorded as a child in `pg_inherits` is refused with `RlsError` before it executes. A rule naming a child table no longer makes that child queryable. A query on the hierarchy's top-level table still runs and returns only rows that match that table's rules, including rows stored in its children.
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured on PostgreSQL or MySQL, and with `database.read_only` true or false, a statement is refused with `RlsError` before it executes when it uses call syntax (`name(...)`, schema-qualified or not) with a name that matches, ignoring case, the name of a routine defined in the database. On PostgreSQL that means any `pg_proc` entry outside the `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` schemas, extension-installed routines included. On MySQL it means any stored function listed in `information_schema.ROUTINES`. Matching uses the routine name alone, across every schema and every argument signature. It covers such calls in the select list, `FROM`, joins, filters, aggregates and window functions, including statements that reference no relation. The names checked are the names called in the SQL that will execute after the RLS rewrite, including calls sqlglot parses as recognized built-in function nodes.
- [ ] While RLS rules are active, the read-only guard's function blocklist applies even when `database.read_only` is false: a statement that calls a function on that blocklist is refused before it executes with `UnsafeSqlError`, which reaches the MCP client as the read-only guard's refusals do today. Only the blocklist check is added on that path; with `database.read_only` false, the statement-type checks (SELECT-only) do not start applying. With no RLS rules configured, behavior for either value of `database.read_only` is unchanged. Unit tests cover, with `database.read_only` false: a blocklisted call under a rule refused; a statement that the RLS rewrite accepts but the SELECT-only checks would refuse (for example a PostgreSQL data-modifying CTE on a table without a rule) not refused by the new check; and a blocklisted call with no rules configured not refused, as today.
- [ ] Functions on the read-only guard's function blocklist are blocked while rules are active, whatever `database.read_only` is: with `database.read_only` true by the existing read-only guard, and with it false by the previous criterion. This change leaves the blocklist's entries as they are; the blocklist additions are delivered in a separate change.
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured, the routine check and the blocklist check do not refuse a statement whose called names are all outside the read-only guard's function blocklist and match no routine name that the database-defined routine check looks up, and such a statement that the other RLS checks accept keeps running with its rule predicates applied. Tests cover at minimum `count(*)` and `upper()` on PostgreSQL and MySQL, plus a PostgreSQL call that sqlglot parses as a typed node with a different canonical name (`strpos`).
- [ ] When a child or routine catalog lookup raises any exception, or the child lookup returns a child flag that is not a boolean, the query is refused with an `RlsError` whose message carries no driver detail. The cause is logged with a traceback, as for the existing relation lookup. A SQL text the check's sqlglot step cannot parse or tokenize is also refused with `RlsError`. The refusal is the same exception type through the same wrappers as the existing view refusal, so it reaches the MCP client exactly as a view refusal does, never as rows.

- [ ] Unit tests in `tests/unit/test_rls_views.py` drive `verify_base_tables` and the PostgreSQL and MySQL runners with fake cursors. A routine lookup that returns no row allows the call.
- [ ] Connector tests in `tests/connectors/test_connectors.py` against real PostgreSQL create two protected parents: a partitioned table with a `PARTITION OF` child, and an ordinary table with an `INHERITS` child. Against real MySQL, they create a stored function that reads the protected table and assert that both the unqualified and the schema-qualified call are blocked. checklist.claim: The internal doc says MySQL partitions are selected inside their table (`FROM orders PARTITION (p0)`) so the rewrite still sees and filters the table, i.e. sqlglot's MySQL parse of a `PARTITION (...)` clause keeps the table node that `apply_rls` scopes and does not error or hide it.
checklist.source_excerpt: MySQL partitions are selected inside their table (`FROM orders PARTITION (p0)`), so the rewrite still sees and filters the table; SQLite has neither.
checklist.verify_against: src/sqllens/safety/rls.py apply_rls table handling under dialect mysql
checklist.verify_hint: Trace `SELECT * FROM orders PARTITION (p0)` with a rule on `orders` through `apply_rls` in `rls.py` and the table-scope walk; confirm the predicate is injected.
checklist.evidence: Traced by reading only; I could not execute sqlglot (no run tool), and the rejection line does not cover this claim. In the installed sqlglot parser (.venv/.../sqlglot/parser.py:1953, 5251-5253) SUPPORTS_PARTITION_SELECTION defaults False, and neither dialects/mysql.py nor any dialect overrides it. So for `FROM orders PARTITION (p0)` the PARTITION clause is not parsed as a partition. PARTITION is in ID_VAR_TOKENS (parser.py:823), so _parse_table_alias (parser.py:4415-4445) most likely reads it as the table alias with column list (p0). If so, the exp.Table node for orders is kept and no ParseError is raised, so apply_rls (rls.py:282-297) would inject the predicate. The qualifier would be table.alias_or_name, i.e. `PARTITION`. The regenerated SQL would then probably be `orders AS PARTITION(p0) WHERE PARTITION.<col> = ...`. That is likely invalid MySQL (it fails, not leaks), and it is not the partition selection the doc describes. No test in the repo exercises this input (grep of tests found none for MySQL PARTITION). The claim that the table is seen and not hidden is plausible, but the doc's wording of how it works is unverified. Without running `sqlglot.parse_one('SELECT * FROM orders PARTITION (p0)', dialect='mysql')` and `apply_rls` I cannot settle it. Command not run: that parse plus apply_rls with a rule on orders under dialect mysql.
